title: Cell theory, microscopes and magnification
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CE01b#t2 term and clue written for the game; CE01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; CE01a#t2 term and clue written for the game; CE01b#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CE01a#N.6, CE01b#N.2, CE01a#N.9, CE01b#N.5, CE01a#N.12, CE01b#N.12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Magnification
items.clue: How many times larger the image is than the object

items.label: Stage micrometer
items.clue: A slide with a real scale, often 1 mm in 100 divisions

items.label: Scale bar
items.clue: A line on an image labelled with the actual length it represents

items.label: Resolution
items.clue: The smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate

questions.stem: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?

options.text: 7.5 µm

questions.explanation: Actual size = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm): the typical diameter of a red blood cell.

questions.stem: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across. They cannot be seen with a light microscope but are clearly visible in electron micrographs. What is the reason?

options.text: Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.
The electron microscope magnifies many more times, so much smaller objects become visible.
Heavy-metal stains used for electron microscopy make small structures much sharper.
Electron microscopes use fluorescent stains that make ribosomes glow in the dark.

questions.explanation: Light limits a light microscope to about 200 nm, so a 25 nm ribosome cannot be resolved; the electron beam's much shorter wavelength gives resolution below 1 nm.

questions.stem: With the ×40 objective lens in place, 40 divisions of an eyepiece graticule line up exactly with 100 µm on a stage micrometer. Using the same objective, a cell spans 44 graticule divisions. What is the actual length of the cell in millimetres?

options.text: 1.1 mm

questions.explanation: 100 µm ÷ 40 = 2.5 µm per division with this objective. 44 × 2.5 µm = 110 µm = 0.11 mm.

questions.stem: A student wants to watch living white blood cells engulfing bacteria about 2 µm long. Which choice of microscope, with its reason, is correct?

options.text: A TEM, as its high resolution would show each step of the engulfing in detail.
An SEM, as its 3D image of the surface would show the cell membrane moving live.
A light microscope, as the cells stay alive and 2 µm is well above its limit.
A light microscope, as extra stain would make the small bacteria appear sharper.

questions.explanation: Living cells can be watched, and bacteria 2 µm long are about ten times larger than the 200 nm resolution limit, so they are clearly resolved.

questions.stem: A micrograph shows a pollen grain 60 mm across. A scale bar on the micrograph is 20 mm long and is labelled 10 µm. What is the actual diameter of the pollen grain?

options.text: 3 µm
30 µm
60 µm
120 µm

questions.explanation: Magnification = 20 000 µm ÷ 10 µm = ×2000. Actual size = 60 000 µm ÷ 2000 = 30 µm.

questions.stem: A virus particle is about 100 nm across. A student photographs a stained sample through a light microscope at ×1500, then enlarges the photo 20 times: a total magnification of ×30 000. At this magnification a 100 nm particle would be 3 mm across. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Its shape will be visible, as anything 3 mm across in a photo can be seen by eye.
Its shape will be visible if more stain is added to make the image sharper.
Its shape will be visible with a higher-power objective instead of enlarging the photo.
No shape will be seen: the particle is below the 200 nm limit, so enlarging only enlarges blur.
